papers.title: Effect of neuB deletion on biofilm formation and extracellular electron transfer in Geobacter sulfurreducens
papers.abstract: The extracellular matrix of Geobacter sulfurreducens biofilms is primarily composed of proteins and exopolysaccharides. The extracellular polymeric substances (EPS) matrix provides the structural scaffold necessary to facilitate extracellular electron transfer (EET); however, the specific role of its carbohydrate components remains unexplored. Sialic acids are a class of carbohydrate derivates that can modulate extracellular matrix stability in bacteria. N-acetylneuraminic acid (Neu5Ac), the most common sialic acid, is primarily synthesized by NeuB. We hypothesized that the neuB gene homolog in G. sulfurreducens (gsu1970), putatively involved in Neu5Ac synthesis, plays a key role in EPS organization and EET performance. Deletion of neuB reduced insoluble Fe(III) oxide reduction by approximately 91%. Furthermore, confocal laser scanning microscopy (CLSM) revealed that the {Delta}neuB strain formed significantly less dense EPS matrices on both hematite and fluorine-doped tin oxide (FTO) electrodes. Interestingly, bioelectrochemical analysis of FTO anodes showed that the mutant produced a 3-fold higher current density and exhibited a more negative open-circuit potential than the wild-type strain. It is important to mention that this enhanced performance on FTO is linked to a significant upregulation of omcS, however, more specific experiments need to be performed to establish a definitive causal relationship between omcS transcription levels and the observed bioelectrochemical enhancement. This transcriptional change was not observed during growth on hematite. Our results suggest that neuB expression contributes to maintaining the structural integrity of the WGA-reactive glycoconjugates within the EPS matrix during insoluble iron reduction. Conversely, its absence is associated with a compensatory upregulation of omcS on FTO electrodes. Overall, this study highlights the potential importance of putative sialic acids-related biosynthetic pathways in Desulfuromonadia, showing that alteration of EPS carbohydrate biosynthetic genes can markedly influence both iron reduction and the performance of electroactive biofilms behavior.

papers.title: A metacommunity of complex microbial communities shows high spatial synchrony, ecological memory, gradual succession and invasion resistance
papers.abstract: Complex microbial communities are increasingly applied in biotechnological and health-related environments, yet maintaining their diversity and relative community composition over extended periods remains challenging. While dispersal can counteract the divergence of spatially separated communities, it remains unclear whether controlled mass transfer can sustain compositional synchrony in highly diverse communities over extended periods, whether this synchrony persist after dispersal is interrupted, and how robust such communities are to invasion. Here, we investigate these questions using a loop-design reactor (LDR) comprising five local wastewater microbial communities connected by controlled mass transfer. The experiment covered multiple rounds of alternating mass transfer and insular phases over a time frame of 318 days, different mass transfer intensities, and the introduction of defined microbial invaders. Community dynamics were monitored at a high temporal resolution by single-cell flow cytometry and complemented by metagenomic analyses of selected samples to characterize taxonomic compositions and functional potential. A Bray-Curtis-based Synchrony Index revealed that controlled mass transfer established high compositional synchrony among five local communities, which persisted for more than 150 generations. Although the community structures underwent gradual succession, the local communities remained synchronized, demonstrating parallel rather than divergent temporal trajectories. Interruption of dispersal initially promote divergence, whereas during later insular phases high compositional similarity persisted in the absence of mass transfer, consistent with ecological memory. Introduced microbial species failed to establish within resident communities, indicating high invasion resistance. Community functional potential remained largely stable throughout the experiment, although phosphorus accumulation failed during phases of high mass transfer. Together, these findings demonstrate that controlled mass transfer can maintain long-term spatial synchrony of complex microbial communities while allowing gradual community succession. Repeated connectivity promoted compositional similarity beyond periods of active dispersal while maintaining invasion resistance and functional stability, highlighting controlled dispersal as a promising community-level strategy for managing complex microbial communities.

papers.title: LuxS Inactivation Increases Antibiotic Susceptibility and Impairs Genetic Competence in Streptococcus pneumoniae
papers.abstract: The LuxS enzyme participates in bacterial metabolism and produces the precursor of autoinducer-2 (AI-2), a signaling molecule implicated in bacterial stress responses and genetic competence. Although LuxS/AI-2 has been associated with antibiotic responses in other streptococci, its contribution to antibiotic susceptibility in Streptococcus pneumoniae remains poorly understood. Here, we investigated the role of LuxS in pneumococcal survival during exposure to erythromycin and ampicillin and examined whether supplementation with 4,5-dihydroxy-2,3-pentanedione (DPD), the precursor of AI-2, could alleviate the effects of luxS inactivation. The {Delta}luxS mutant exhibited significantly greater reductions in viable cell counts than the wild type following antibiotic exposure, even after accounting for differences in baseline growth. Supplementation with 50 nM DPD significantly improved mutant survival during exposure to both antibiotics. We further investigated the contribution of LuxS/AI-2 to genetic competence, a phenotype previously associated with luxS inactivation. The mutant exhibited reduced transformation efficiency, which was significantly improved by DPD supplementation, although recovery remained partial. Together, these findings provide evidence that LuxS contributes to pneumococcal survival during antibiotic exposure and demonstrate that exogenous DPD can partially compensate for the effects of luxS inactivation on antibiotic responses and genetic transformation. These results extend our understanding of LuxS/AI-2-associated phenotypes in S. pneumoniae.

papers.title: Reconstitution in JCVI-syn3B suggests the roles of the Spiroplasma Fibril protein (Sfibril) in swimming
papers.abstract: Spiroplasma, wall-less helical bacteria of the class Mollicutes, swim without flagella by shifting the handedness of their helical body. This motility is driven by an internal ribbon composed of actin-superfamily MreB proteins (SMreB) and the Spiroplasma-specific Fibril protein (Sfibril), which accounts for nearly half of the ribbon mass. However, because helical shape and swimming have been reconstituted with SMreBs alone, the role of Sfibril has remained unclear. Here, we expressed Fibril from Spiroplasma eriocheiris under its native promoter in the minimal synthetic bacterium JCVI-syn3B (syn3), in which swimming had been reconstituted with SMreB proteins, and analyzed cell morphology and swimming. Sfibril formed filaments with chained ring units in syn3 cells and, by itself, induced cell elongation and left-handed helical shape. Elongated cells expressing Sfibril recovered their length after hypo-osmotic shock, indicating that Sfibril confers morphological robustness. In cells expressing SMreB4 and SMreB5 from Spiroplasma, Sfibril increased the fraction of helical and motile cells, extended the distance of continuous kink propagation, reduced cell bending, and increased traveling distance. In addition, Sfibril altered the handedness of SMreB5-driven helices from exclusively right-handed to a mixture of right- and left-handed. These results suggest that Sfibril is not essential for helicity shift but stabilizes the cell body and supports efficient, processive helicity shifts.

papers.title: Charting the Expansive Outer Membrane β-Barrel Landscape in Pseudomonas aeruginosa
papers.abstract: Outer-membrane beta-barrel (OMBB) proteins are central to Gram-negative bacterial physiology, mediating nutrient acquisition and secretion while shaping host interactions and antimicrobial permeability. Yet tools to catalog the diversity and functional potential of the OMBB proteome in these bacteria remain incompletely defined. Here, we combine proteome-scale structure prediction analysis and experimental validation to systematically map the OMBB proteome of the opportunistic pathogen Pseudomonas aeruginosa. We identify 105 proteins containing predicted OMBB domains with 8-26 beta-strands, substantially expanding the repertoire across major structural classes and revealing previously unrecognised domain architectures. Comparison with experimentally defined structures shows that prediction accurately captures global barrel architecture but systematically overestimates beta-strand continuity and underrepresents flexible extracellular loops, key determinants of molecular recognition. We then defined the cryo-EM structures of PA2590 and PA3535 (EprS), confirming their predicted functions as a TonB-dependent transporter and an autotransporter, respectively. Using structural prediction, we also identified the phospholipase A1-like activity in the uncharacterized autotransporter PA4579, linking a predicted catalytic site to function. Together, our findings expand the structural and functional landscape of the P. aeruginosa OMBB proteome and establish a generalizable framework for converting proteome-scale structural predictions into experimentally testable mechanisms, enabling discovery of functions hidden within poorly annotated outer-membrane proteomes.

papers.title: Resistome-based machine learning source attribution of a superbug
papers.abstract: Many bacterial human pathogens infect not only humans but also other species, and source attribution has been very useful for studying transmission among the different sources. Yet, critical pathogens such as Acinetobacter baumannii have not been studied using source attribution approaches. Here, we conducted machine source attribution using the resistome of almost 1200 A. baumannii genomes from four sources: humans, companion animals , soil, and white storks. Of note, no other study has used the resistome as input data before. First, we selected the best model among 168 parameter combinations, which was Random Forest, with 5-fold cross-validation and chi2 for feature selection. The model shows a reasonably good accuracy with an F1 weighted score = 0.744, yet class accuracy was dependent on the source. Whereas for companion animals and humans, 93% and 86% of the predictions were correct, respectively; the other two categories (soil and white stork) show correct predictions below 50%. Yet, a core phylogeny and ST assignment reveal that the wrong predictions are associated with multi-host lineages. Finally, we identify the most important ARGs contributing to each class prediction and, in the case of companion animals, tetgenes, which confer resistance to tetracycline, were among the top contributors. Our study shows the resistome's potential for developing models to predict source associations. More broadly, this study shows how integrating machine learning and phylogenomics can help us understand multi-host transmission dynamics.

papers.title: Compartment-associated filtering and environmental gradients shape fungal communities in arid Artemisia species
papers.abstract: Plant-associated fungal communities are shaped by interactions among host, environmental conditions, and compartment-specific filtering processes, yet the relative importance of these drivers remains poorly understood in arid and semi-arid ecosystems. We investigated fungal communities associated with three Artemisia species (Artemisia herba-alba Asso., Artemisia mesatlantica Maire and Artemisia negrei L.), including Moroccan endemics, across bulk soil, rhizosphere, root, and shoot compartments using ITS amplicon sequencing, culture-dependent isolation, and ecological analyses. Fungal community composition differed significantly among compartments (PERMANOVA, R2 = 0.08, P = 0.012), whereas alpha diversity showed limited variation. Taxonomic profiles revealed compartment-associated shifts, with recurrent fungal genera concentrated in belowground compartments and a higher proportion of unclassified taxa in shoots. Core microbiome analyses identified overlapping fungal taxa between rhizosphere and root communities. Soil physicochemical gradients were associated with fungal community composition, and structural equation modeling indicated significant associations with both environmental variables and plant compartments. Source-tracking analysis attributed approximately 99.4% of root community composition to rhizosphere sources, whereas shoot communities showed contributions from both roots (60%) and the rhizosphere (39%). Culture-dependent isolation recovered 21 fungal isolates, with five genera shared between cultivation and sequencing datasets. Together, these findings reveal compartment-associated fungal community restructuring along the soil?plant continuum and highlight the complementary contributions of environmental conditions, plant-associated habitats, and cultivation-based characterization to understanding fungal microbiomes in arid ecosystems.

papers.title: Host HSP90 mimicry by a parasite effector triggers mitochondrial membrane shedding
papers.abstract: The outer mitochondrial membrane mediates critical host defenses against intracellular pathogens. How microbes manipulate this compartment remains poorly understood. Here, we found that the human parasite Toxoplasma gondii remodels host mitochondrial membranes through molecular mimicry of HSP90 chaperones. Cryo-electron microscopy analyses showed that the parasite effector TgMAF1 binds the same specialized clamp domain of the mitochondrial import receptor TOM70 as chaperones of the HSP70/90 family. Biochemical and comparative genomics analyses demonstrate that this mimicry arose through the neofunctionalization of the TgMAF1 C-terminus from an ancestral paralog incapable of TOM70 binding. In molecular dynamics simulations, complexed TgMAF1-TOM70 triggered the formation of higher order assemblies that induced local membrane curvature. These findings uncover a previously unknown host subversion strategy and establish molecular mimicry of a chaperone as a mechanism for pathogen-driven remodeling of the host OMM.

papers.title: Tissue-specific genomic and transcriptomic dynamics of the OsHV-1 lytic cycle in the Pacific oyster Magallana gigas revealed by long-read sequencing
papers.abstract: Ostreid herpesvirus 1 (OsHV-1) causes recurrent mass mortality of juvenile Pacific oysters (Magallana gigas) worldwide, yet its lytic cycle remains poorly characterized in vivo. In the absence of a permissive cell line, most studies have relied on intramuscular injection, which bypasses the natural route of infection, or on primary haemocyte cultures, which cannot capture tissue-level host-virus interactions. In addition, gene expression studies have relied on short-read sequencing, which fragments transcription units and cannot resolve complex transcriptional architectures. Long-read sequencing has recently revealed abundant overlapping, antisense and polycistronic transcripts in other herpesviruses, but whether OsHV-1 shares this complexity, and how its transcriptional program varies across host tissues during natural infection, remains unknown. Here, we exposed naive oysters to OsHV-1 by bath exposure and combined long-read genomic and transcriptomic sequencing of gills, mantle, digestive gland and adductor muscle at increasing levels of infection. OsHV-1 genomes were assembled directly from infected tissues, and intra-host viral diversity was structured by host rather than tissue. We identified 410 unspliced viral transcripts, including overlapping, antisense and polycistronic transcripts. The viral transcriptional program was largely conserved across tissues and resembled that previously described in haemocytes in vitro. In the host, infection triggered a response shared by all tissues, but earlier and stronger in the gills and mantle. Together, these results provide the first long-read view of the OsHV-1 lytic cycle in its natural host.

papers.title: Genomic and phenotypic characterisation of Penicillium melinii, a plant growth-promoting root endophyte that remains effective under salt stress
papers.abstract: Penicillium melinii isolate 2 is a root endophyte of Arabidopsis thaliana that promotes the growth of different plant species, but the genetic basis of this activity remains unknown. Here we combined Oxford Nanopore long reads and Illumina short reads to obtain a high-quality, near-chromosome-level assembly of 29.39 Mb in six nuclear scaffolds, two of them telomere-capped at both ends (97.6% complete BUSCOs), together with, to our knowledge, the first complete mitochondrial genome reported for the species (26,730 bp). Annotation predicted 9,566 protein-coding genes. Compared with two other plant growth-promoting Penicillium species, P. bilaiae and P. citrinum, the isolate encodes fewer carbohydrate-active enzymes, biosynthetic gene clusters and candidate effectors, pointing to an overall reduction of the secreted repertoire. In vitro, the isolate grew significantly above the control on 63 of 95 carbon sources, mainly carbohydrates, and was positive for 7 of 11 plant growth-promoting traits: siderophore production, phosphate and zinc solubilisation, ammonia release, and urease, proteolytic and lipolytic activities. Radial growth was unaffected by NaCl up to 150 mM and persisted at 1 M, whereas conidiation was more salt-sensitive. On medium containing 100 mM NaCl, inoculation increased Arabidopsis shoot fresh weight and root system growth. Genome mining identified candidate genes for these traits. Together, these results provide a genomic and phenotypic basis for evaluating P. melinii isolate 2 as an inoculant for saline soils and identify candidate determinants for functional validation.

papers.title: Defining host factors required for dengue virus NS1-induced endothelial hyperpermeability and endothelial glycocalyx layer disruption
papers.abstract: Dengue virus (DENV) is a mosquito-borne positive-sense RNA virus belonging to the Flaviviridae family that poses a significant threat to global health. Clinical manifestations of DENV infection range from febrile to severe disease characterized by vascular leakage. The secreted DENV nonstructural protein 1 (NS1) contributes to endothelial dysfunction through interactions with endothelial cells, leading to disruption of the endothelial glycocalyx and intercellular junction complexes (IJC). However, host factors required for NS1-triggered endothelial dysfunction are not well understood. It is also unclear if NS1 highjacks different host factors and signaling pathways for glycocalyx and IJC disruption. To address these questions, we used a targeted genetic approach to identify host factors required either for NS1-triggered endothelial glycocalyx layer (EGL) disruption, as assessed by immunofluorescence assays, or for IJC disruption, as measured by transendothelial electrical resistance. After demonstrating the decoupled nature of EGL and IJC disruption in our models, we genetically depleted host factors with known roles in regulating endothelial barrier function and/or involvement in NS1 pathogenesis, including heparanase, cathepsin L, sialidases, and the PI3K/AKT/mTOR and {beta}-catenin signaling pathways. Our results reveal a complex genetic landscape where NS1-induced disruption of EGL and IJCs involves both unique and shared host factors. Further, our data identify a direct role for {beta}-catenin in NS1-induced endothelial dysfunction in vitro and in vivo. Overall, this work advances understanding of host factors required for DENV NS1-triggered endothelial dysfunction, revealing distinct intracellular pathways that are highjacked by NS1 to modulate barrier function, thus providing new insights into dengue-associated vascular leak.

papers.title: Genomic reassessment of Enterobacter species and subspecies
papers.abstract: Enterobacter species are opportunistic pathogens whose identification is complicated by closely related lineages and changing species nomenclature. We reassessed 1,074 public genomes using average nucleotide identity (ANI), type-strain comparisons and phylogenies based on conserved markers, genome alignments and k-mers. Among 1,070 genomes included in the classification comparison, 123 changed species or subspecies membership relative to NCBI labels, 499 changed names following revisions to species boundaries or ranks, and 69 previously unnamed genomes received species assignments. The oharae, steigerwaltii, xiangfangensis and hoffmannii lineages formed an expanded Enterobacter xiangfangensis, separate from the lineage containing the E. hormaechei type. We propose five transferred combinations: E. xiangfangensis subsp. oharae comb. nov., E. xiangfangensis subsp. steigerwaltii comb. nov., E. xiangfangensis subsp. hoffmannii comb. nov., E. roggenkampii subsp. quasiroggenkampii comb. nov. and E. chengduensis subsp. rongchengensis comb. nov. We also describe the corresponding type subspecies, E. xiangfangensis subsp. xiangfangensis comb. nov., E. roggenkampii subsp. roggenkampii comb. nov. and E. chengduensis subsp. chengduensis comb. nov., and emend the descriptions of E. xiangfangensis and E. hormaechei. E. dykesii and E. quasimori are treated as later heterotypic synonyms of E. asburiae and E. mori, respectively. Within E. xiangfangensis subsp. hoffmannii, we define 25 genomic groups (genomovars) at 99.5% ANI. Conflicting tree relationships leave the position of E. ludwigii and the branching order of the hoffmannii-associated types unresolved. We developed Pterobacter to apply the revised classifications to assemblies, using alignment-based ANI near the species boundary and withholding assignments when the reference evidence is insufficient.

papers.title: In vivo crosslinking and cryo-EM analyses suggest a revised model of conjugative pilus biogenesis
papers.abstract: Bacterial conjugation requires elaboration of a conjugative pilus by membrane-embedded transport machineries known as Type IV Secretion Systems (T4SSs). Recent structural findings suggested a model of conjugative pilus biogenesis in which the pilus is assembled from the VirB6-base of the T4SS Stalk, while the VirB5-apex is projected at the pilus tip. In this study, we show that in vivo crosslinking of these two Stalk segments within the R388 T4SS has only a modest effect on conjugative transfer efficiency, inconsistent with them separating during pilus elaboration. Combined with cryo-electron microscopy analyses of the homologous pKM101 T4SS, this leads us to propose a revised model, in which the sixfold-symmetrical inner membrane complex of the T4SS serves directly as a base for assembly of the fivefold-symmetrical pilus. The resulting symmetry mismatch is resolved by the sequential incorporation of pilus subunits at a continuously repositioning gap at the base of the nascent pilus. This revised model answers the long-standing question of how T4SSs accommodate a central symmetry mismatch during a crucial process of bacterial conjugation underpinning horizontal gene transfer.

papers.title: Modular evolution and functional divergence of the Pseudomonas Fit toxin locus
papers.abstract: The insecticidal Fit toxin is well known for its role in insect interactions in plant-associated Pseudomonas. However, its presence in non-entomopathogenic Pseudomonas, including the marine fish pathogen Pseudomonas baetica, raises questions about its evolutionary history and functional diversification. Here, we investigate the fit locus across the Pseudomonas fluorescens species complex using comparative genomic, structural, and functional approaches. Phylogenomic analyses support several ancient acquisitions of the fit gene cluster, followed by Pseudomonas subgroup-specific chromosomal integration and diversification of the toxin FitD and the sensor kinase FitF. Although P. baetica carries a fit operon, it showed no oral toxicity toward insect larvae. This lack of toxicity is associated with resistance to gut colonization by the commensal Enterobacter sp. Direct hemolymph injection also failed to reveal toxicity and the Fit activity in P. baetica is limited by the absence of fit promoter activation in insect hemolymph. Finally, in a zebrafish model, FitD is dispensable for P. baetica, which causes severe systemic infection through other virulence mechanisms. Nonetheless, FitD contributes to the virulence of P. protegens CHA0 in zebrafish, thereby extending its effects from insects to vertebrate hosts. Together, these findings highlight the evolutionary and regulatory plasticity of the fit locus and show how an ancestral toxin system can acquire different functional roles in bacteria adapted to distinct ecological niches.

papers.title: Microbial communities do not drive chronic Quercus spp. decline but exacerbate tree weakening: a multi kingdom soil root continuum study in Chantilly forest
papers.abstract: In European forests, several species of Quercus spp. are currently subject to major declines, defined as a slow deterioration of the tree caused by the interaction of abiotic and biotic factors, in which drought often plays an important role. The decline of holobionts, like oak trees, may have consequences that extend beyond the tree physiology. To better understand the interactions between chronic oak decline and oak associated microbial communities and their functional consequences, we analysed the bacterial, fungal and oomycetes communities in the bulk soil, the rhizosphere and the roots of pairs of declining and non-declining oaks in the Chantilly forest (France) by a metabarcoding approach. Chosen pairs of oaks were distributed on contrasted soil types to determine the influence of soil properties on the tree-microbe interactions during decline. Rhizospheric soil microbial enzymatic activities were also measured to assess the effect of oak decline on microbial-driven nutrient cycling activities. We observed a differential response of microbial communities to decline as a function of the kingdom. Bacteria were more sensitive to oak decline, particularly in the bulk soil and on podzol soil. By contrast, the composition of fungal communities was overall little impacted by oak decline, no matter the soil type, but their functional abilities may be partly impaired. Laccase and chitinase activities were reduced in the rhizospheric soil of declining oaks growing on brunisol and luvisol. Furthermore, the proportion of ectomycorrhizal fungi with high biomass exploration types were reduced by half in the roots of declining trees while the pathogenic Phytophthora cactorum and P. plurivora were more frequent. Altogether, our data suggest that chronic oak decline affects directly and indirectly the composition and functional abilities of oak associated microbial communities in a soil dependent manner.

papers.title: A host-pathogen tug-of-war over migrasome biogenesis in Vibrio cholerae infection
papers.abstract: Migrasomes are extracellular organelles implicated in cell communication and immune signaling, yet their induction by bacterial toxins and functional consequences during infection remains unknown. Here, we show that Vibrio cholerae infection induces non-canonical migracytosis in multiple cell types through the MARTX toxin. The actin cross-linking domain (ACD) promotes cell contraction and retraction fiber formation, while the /{beta}-hydrolase domain (ABH) collaborates with actin-polymerization machinery to support migrasome maturation. The Rho inactivation domain (RID) covalently modifies multiple Rho/Ras GTPases, and its absence yields oversized membrane blebs (large vesicles) enriched in endoplasmic reticulum, lipid droplets, and pro-inflammatory chemokines compared with wild-type migrasomes. In an infant mouse model, RID-deficient V. cholerae exhibits impaired intestinal colonization and elevated host chemokine transcription. These findings establish that MARTX-driven migrasome formation is not merely a byproduct of cytoskeleton damage, but represents a coordinated, domain-specific reprogramming of host membrane dynamics with implications for host-pathogen interplay.

papers.title: Barley malting for beer production - Impact of temperature on the barley-associated microbiome, malt quality and energy expenditure.
papers.abstract: Malt production is an energy-intensive process, and elevated germination temperatures have been proposed to shorten it and thereby lower the energy demand. However, the effect of elevated temperatures on the barley-associated microbiome remains unexplored. Using a multi-metaomics approach, we explored microbial composition and function in four barley varieties malted at pilot scale under standard industrial conditions (IMR) and an accelerated regime using higher temperatures (AMR). AMR yielded malts with excellent friability, resulting in adequate wort viscosity and saccharification times despite lower amylase and beta-glucanase activities, with no effect on proteolysis modulation. AMR substantially shifted microbial community composition. Fungi, notably Alternaria alternata, contributed xylan- and beta-glucan-degrading enzymes, whereas abundant detection of the strong biofilm former Pseudomonas coincided with impaired wort filtration. Electrical energy use was lowered in AMR by approximately 5-9%, mainly through lower humidification and cooling demand. Malting with increased temperatures thus promises high-quality malt with time and energy savings, provided that the malting microbiome is monitored and controlled.

papers.title: Agricultural Management Restructures the Functional Composition of Soil Fungal Communities Across Tropical Landscapes
papers.abstract: Soil fungal communities regulate key ecosystem processes, yet the extent to which agricultural management restructures fungal diversity across tropical landscapes remains poorly understood. We characterized fungal communities in 124 soil samples collected from natural vegetation, organic farms, and non-organic farms across four Honduran departments using internal transcribed spacer 2 (ITS2) and small-subunit ribosomal RNA (SSU) metabarcoding. Land use was associated with Bray-Curtis community composition after adjusting for geography, sequencing run, and read depth (ITS2 R2 = 0.06, SSU R2 = 0.05, both P < 0.001). Community dissimilarity increased with geographic distance within each land-use category (pooled Mantel r = 0.30 for ITS2 and 0.19 for SSU), and land-use categories shared 2.0-7.1 times as many fungal features as expected (all adjusted P < 0.001). For ITS2, total richness in non-organic soils was 18% lower than in natural soils and 25% lower than in organic soils. Across both markers, land-use restricted richness was 58-85% lower in non-organic soils than in natural and organic soils. In addition, symbiotrophs in non-organic soils were 18-20% of that in natural soils, while saprotroph and pathotroph responses varied by marker. Together, these findings demonstrate that agricultural management is associated with changes in fungal diversity, occupancy, and predicted trophic composition without eliminating the geographic structure or extensive taxonomic overlap of regional communities.

papers.title: The dynamic expressome of Pseudomonas putida: condition-dependent remodelling of the RNA polymerase interactome
papers.abstract: As in many bacteria, the 2{beta}{beta}'{omega} core RNA polymerase (RNAP) of Pseudomonas putida interacts in vivo with sigma factors, transcriptional regulators and auxiliary proteins whose relative abundance varies with the physiological state. Here, we used an in vivo immunocapture approach to examine condition-dependent changes in the RNAP interactome of P. putida KT2440. His-, Myc- and E-tags were separately introduced at the C-terminus of RpoC ({beta}'), a permissive, surface-exposed site accessible to cognate antibodies. Myc-tagged RNAP complexes were immunocaptured with magnetic beads and analyzed by LC-ESI-MS/MS and computational methods. The results revealed condition-dependent association of the RNAP core (RpoA, RpoB, RpoC and RpoZ) with distinct pools of sigma factors, as well as ribosomal proteins, RNA-processing factors and metabolic enzymes. Nutrient starvation, nutrient-rich growth and high temperature altered the composition and relative representation of RNAP-associated proteins. Despite the limited physiological conditions examined, our results support a model in which RNAP acts as a dynamic organizational hub of the bacterial expressome, integrating transcription with translation, RNA maturation and central metabolism.

papers.title: Taxogenomic resolution of the 16SrIII (X-disease) group: elevation of Candidatus Phytoplasma pruni-related strains to species rank and proposal of three novel Candidatus species Candidatus Phytoplasma caryae sp. nov., Candidatus Phytoplasma conii sp. nov. and Candidatus Phytoplasma lactucae sp. nov.
papers.abstract: Alongside the proposal of the taxon Candidatus Phytoplasma pruni for 16SrIII (X-Disease) group, the designation Candidatus Phytoplasma pruni-related strains was proposed for strains that were closely related to the taxon based on multilocus sequence characterization. However, recent genome-based studies have created taxonomic ambiguity by either assigning related strains directly to the taxon Ca. P. pruni or separating them into more than one genomic cluster without formal taxonomic classification or proposing new taxon for new divergent strains. In this study, we sequenced genomes of the pecan bunchy top phytoplasma (PBT), previously designated a Ca. P. pruni-related strain, initially to confirm the pathogen in an Oklahoma pecan orchard. Phylogenomic comparisons with previously sequenced Candidatus Phytoplasma pruni strains revealed four well-supported taxonomic groups based on average nucleotide identity, digital DNA-DNA hybridization, and phylogenetic analyses, with different host ecologies consistent with International Research Programme on Comparative Mycoplasmology (IRPCM) guidelines for assigning new taxon. Accordingly, we propose a reclassification of Ca. P. pruni and related strains into four species: Candidatus Phytoplasma pruni, representing the taxon associated with X-disease phytoplasma; three proposed new Candidatus species including Candidatus Phytoplasma caryae sp. nov, Candidatus Phytoplasma conii sp. nov and Candidatus Phytoplasma lactucae sp. nov. The study provides comparative-genomic insights into these taxonomic groups that support their evolution.

papers.title: Three novel deep-branching orphan protist lineages from the marine rare biosphere
papers.abstract: Metabarcoding has transformed our view of marine protist communities, yet many sequences in environmental surveys are not assigned confident taxonomic identity. These taxonomically ambiguous sequences may include lineages that are not within any known eukaryotic supergroup, which we refer to here as orphan lineages. These orphan lineages matter beyond taxonomy-based community analyses, because they can help us understand early eukaryotic evolution. Here we used phylogenetic inferences and sequence similarity networks (SSNs) of long-read metabarcoding data of the ribosomal operon (18S-28S rDNA) to identify three novel phylum-level orphan lineages. We designate these lineages Deep Orphan Lineages 1-3 (DEEPOLs) and show that they are exclusively marine and part of the rare biosphere, yet ecologically distinct: DEEPOL1 is a cosmopolitan generalist, DEEPOL2 a conditionally rare lineage capable of local polar blooms, and DEEPOL3 a non-polar lineage with a tendency toward the dark ocean. For DEEPOL2, lineage-specific digital PCR (dPCR) combined with catalyzed reporter deposition fluorescence in situ hybridization (CARD-FISH) provides the first in situ visualization of these cells, revealing small, flagellated, and morphologically inconspicuous protists. Together, our results show that substantial diversity remains hidden among rare lineages, and that long-read sequencing combined with targeted molecular and microscopy approaches offers a first step toward linking orphan sequences to organisms and their evolution and ecological roles.

papers.title: Single-cell genomics reveals genomic and functional differentiation between freshwater and saline Achromatium populations.
papers.abstract: Giant sulfur bacteria of the genus Achromatium reportedly contain extensive genomic diversity within individual cells. Most genomic data (35 assemblies) come from freshwater populations obtained from Lake Stechlin, Germany, alongside four single-cell genomes from a salt marsh and saline mineral springs. Here, we characterize marine Achromatium from mangrove sediments in Guadeloupe and compare them with freshwater and saline references. Microscopy, elemental mapping, and Raman spectroscopy revealed calcium-rich inclusions, and intracellular elemental sulfur as previously described for this genus. Scanning electron microscopy revealed two cell-size morphotypes. We generated eleven single-cell, four mixed-cell, and two metagenomic binned assemblies from Guadeloupe mangrove. Divergent copies of conserved marker genes revealed extensive intracellular genomic diversity in individual cells of both morphotypes. Multigene phylogenies provided separation between freshwater references and most genomes from saline environments, including the Guadeloupe population. Gene presence-absence analyses further revealed differences in functional potential between Guadeloupe and Stechlin cells across five functional annotation categories including PFAM, KEGG Orthologs, and CAZymes. Differences in genes associated with osmotic regulation, ion transport, carbohydrate degradation, and secretion systems suggest variation in functional potential related to environmental adaptation, interactions and resource utilization. No significant differences in functional potential between Guadeloupe morphotypes were found. Together, these marine genomes reveal genomic and functional differentiation from freshwater populations and suggest that intracellular diversity does not erase freshwater/saline population boundaries.

papers.title: Depolymerases unmask a conserved receptor to enable phage control of capsulated Acinetobacter baumannii
papers.abstract: We characterized bacteriophage Abs1 that infects clinical Acinetobacter baumannii isolates via the highly prevalent and conserved outer-membrane protein receptor, OprC. However, phage Abs1 is unable to infect capsulated A. baumannii strains as the capsule prevents phage access to its underlying receptor. To circumvent this, we combined phage Abs1 with recombinant depolymerases targeting the major A. baumannii capsule types. In a murine bacteremia model, this combination significantly reduced bacterial burden caused by diverse, capsulated A. baumannii strains.

papers.title: Choosing between Glycolysis and Cholera: identifying glycolipid- and enzyme-based markers of extracellular vesicles in non-model organisms
papers.abstract: The lack of universal markers for extracellular vesicles (EVs) is delaying progress in the field, especially research using non-model organisms. To develop effective options for the detection of EVs, we explored glycolipid-based and protein-based markers. In this study, we show that cholera toxin subunit B (CTxb), which targets the glycosphingolipid GM1 in vertebrates, also binds to EVs from various non-model organisms enabling detection. However, whilst CTxb selectively detect EVs from cell culture and parasite media, it is unsuitable for complex biofluids, such as serum and plasma due to cross-reactivity with high- and low-density lipoproteins. Additionally, we show that the universally conserved glycolytic enzyme enolase is found in EVs from phylogenetically distant species. Multiple highly conserved regions exist across human and several representative non-model organism orthologues, enabling detection of EVs from non-model organism using antibodies against human enolase. Furthermore, the conserved enzymatic activity of enolase enables detection of EVs using an enzymatic assay. Together CTxb and enolase provide a tandem approach for detection of EVs from non-model organisms by targeting different, conserved components of EVs.

papers.title: Enhancing violacein production in an Antarctic bacterial strain: New opportunities for biomedical use
papers.abstract: Violacein is a valuable bioactive metabolite produced by diverse bacteria, including the Antarctic isolate Janthinobacterium sp. UV13. Despite its broad therapeutic potential, large-scale production in native producers is hindered by low yields and the concurrent synthesis of exopolysaccharides, which increases downstream processing complexity and costs. This study employed a sequential statistical approach to optimize culture parameters, enhancing violacein productivity while minimizing exopolysaccharides production in UV13. The methodology included carbon and nitrogen source screening, a Plackett Burman design and a concentration response optimization, followed by chemical inducers evaluation. Results demonstrated that sucrose was an effective carbon source (violacein yield: 32.75 mg/L). Inorganic nitrogen significantly favored violacein synthesis (yield: 28 mg/L, p < 0.05) over organic alternatives which reduced violacein yields 3.4 to 4.2 fold. A single factor central composite design of ammonium sulfate concentration yielded a formulation producing 75.8 mg/L of violacein with an exopolysaccharide titer of 0.91 mg/L. Furthermore, tryptophan was the better inducer, increasing violacein production 2.2 fold (p < 0.05) while simultaneously decreasing exopolysaccharides formation 4.5 fold. The new formulated medium significantly outperformed previously reported conditions, demonstrating that parameter manipulation unlocks UV13 biosynthetic potential for scalable violacein production.

papers.title: Spatial growth within food-like matrices drives physiological diversification and stress adaptation in Salmonella.
papers.abstract: Foodborne bacteria often grow in structured environments, but the effects of spatial organisation on their physiology and subsequent stress tolerance remain poorly understood. In this study, we investigated how spatial growth in a food-like hydrogel matrix affected the physiology of Salmonella enterica serovar Typhimurium and its ability to cope with environmental stresses. Planktonic and spatialised populations were grown for four days in media without NaCl supplementation or supplemented with 6% NaCl. Transcriptomic, extracellular metabolomic, and lipidomic analyses were combined with targeted spatial gene-expression analyses. The multi-omics analyses showed that spatial organisation had a strong effect on Salmonella physiology and induce more physiological variation than the presence of osmotic stress, under the tested conditions. Spatial growth was associated with significant changes in gene expression, carbon metabolism, and membrane fatty-acid composition. Several functions related to stress response and biofilm-associated behaviour were also affected, with corresponding genes showing significant differential expression. When bacteria were grown in the presence of NaCl, spatialised populations showed less transcriptional and metabolic reorganisation than planktonic populations. In addition, gene-expression analyses showed that microcolonies were physiologically heterogeneous, with differences among cell populations within the same microcolony. Spatial growth also associated with the upregulation of functions related to the general stress response, oxidative stress protection, membrane adaptation and acid stress. These physiological changes provide a plausible mechanistic framework for the enhanced gastrointestinal stress tolerance previously observed in spatially grown populations, particularly under acid challenge. Overall, our results show that spatial organisation is an important environmental factor that reprograms Salmonella physiology and can influence its ability to survive stresses encountered after food ingestion.

papers.title: Endogenous serine proteases in MDCK sublines support trypsin-independent influenza A virus replication
papers.abstract: The haemagglutinin (HA) of influenza A viruses (IAV) must be proteolytically cleaved by trypsin-like proteases to mediate fusion between the viral envelope and endosomal membrane of the host cell, a crucial step in virus entry. Most established cell lines rely on exogenous trypsin for the multicycle replication of influenza A viruses. In this study, we investigated various sublines of Madin-Darby canine kidney (MDCK) cells and found that MDCK-NBL2, MDCK-I, and MDCK-II support trypsin-independent replication of various influenza A viruses, including human, porcine, and avian strains. The serine protease inhibitors camostat and nafamostat mesylate reduced viral replication in a dose-dependent manner. However, the inhibitory effect diminished with increasing viral dose, most likely due to competition between the HA and the inhibitors for binding on the protease. We detected the endogenous expression of several transmembrane serine proteases in MDCK sublines, including TMPRSS2 and TMPRSS4. The characterization of these two canine serine proteases showed that TMPRSS4, but not TMPRSS2, is mainly localizing to the plasma membrane. Furthermore, canine TMPRSS4 was more effective than TMPRSS2 in terms of proteolytic activation of various influenza viruses, although there were strain-dependent differences. These results indicate that certain MDCK sublines express functional HA-activating proteases, providing useful models for the replication of influenza viruses without exogenous trypsin, as well as for the evaluation of antiviral strategies targeting transmembrane serine proteases.

papers.title: Recovery of a distant large DNA virus from the genome sequencing of a fish leech
papers.abstract: The leech gut is known to be a viral reservoir, where viruses can persist long-term and are protected from external influences. Therefore, leeches can serve as vectors for transmission of viral disease to susceptible hosts on which they prey. Nonetheless, viral diversity and virus-leech-host interactions remain largely unknown, with hitherto no research directed at identifying viruses that use leeches as their hosts. In the present study, we report the discovery of a novel large DNA virus (phylum Nucleocytoviricota) recovered from genomic sequencing data of the common fish leech Piscicola geometra (Linnaeus, 1761). Through genomic and phylogenetic analyses, we identify this lineage as highly divergent from currently known viruses, with [~]95% of its predicted protein-coding genes showing no identifiable homology with current databases. Whether the leech is a host of this virus or a vector that transmits it to fish species remains unclear. This work highlights the value of off-target sequence retrieval for discovering novel viral lineages and sets the stage for future studies directed towards the prevalence and biology of leech-associated large DNA viruses.

papers.title: Illumina MiSeq, MiSeq i100, and Element AVITI yield concordant ecological patterns for universal 16S and 18S rRNA gene amplicon sequencing
papers.abstract: Molecular microbiome analyses require high-resolution, comparable measurements, often obtained by sequencing marker genes such as the rRNA gene. Recently, new platforms and chemistries have promised to improve performance at lower cost relative to the commonly used Illumina MiSeq 2x300, but have not yet been systematically compared especially for rRNA gene amplicon studies. Here, we compared MiSeq 2x300, MiSeq 2x500, and AVITI 2x300 by sequencing mock communities and field samples via a 'universal' (16S + 18S) rRNA gene amplicons (V4-V5 region) approach. All platforms recovered similar community patterns (Mantel r > 0.93), with no major differences in recovered lineages. MiSeq 2x500 showed ~4.5-fold higher index hopping (5.9 +/- 3.8% vs. 1.3 +/- 1.5%). For 18S, MiSeq 2x500, despite longer reads overlapping the 18S V4-V5 region, only marginally improved taxonomic classification (+0.7% on average) and ASV resolution (+/-1.3%). Meanwhile, all platforms similarly biased against 18S due to its greater length, which we demonstrate can be offset by a gel-based size selection, with no apparent taxonomic bias. Overall the platforms yield ecologically similar results. We highlight platform-specific advantages to help guide decision-making and challenges that can be addressed through dedicated bioinformatic or wet-lab approaches.

papers.title: A conserved MoxR-vWA chaperone complex drives starvation-induced protein degradation in bacteria
papers.abstract: Bacteria must quickly adapt to changes in their environment, notably including the sudden loss of nutrients. We previously showed that in glucose-starved E. coli, widespread starvation-induced protein degradation (SPD) fuels post-starvation proteome remodeling, degrading a wide swath of the proteome to supply the cell with energy and amino acids for synthesis of stress proteins. Here we demonstrate that SPD is mediated by a highly conserved complex of three proteins: the MoxR-type AAA+ ATPase SpdA, the von Willebrand factor A (vWA) domain protein SpdB, and the zinc metallopeptidase SpdC. Structural modeling and in vitro reconstitutions show that these proteins form a complex with 6:1:1 stoichiometry that resembles the widespread, but still poorly understood, family of MoxR-vWA chaperone complexes in bacteria and eukaryotes. Measurements of protein degradation in glucose-starved E. coli cells show that SpdA, SpdB, and SpdC work together to mediate the degradation of SPD substrates. Instead of directly degrading these substrates, our data suggest that limited structural perturbation and proteolysis "softens" SPD substrates and promotes their degradation by the cellular proteases ClpAP/ClpXP and Lon. Thus, SPD enables extensive proteome remodeling during starvation by expanding the pool of proteins accessible to cellular proteases, rather than by increasing protease abundance. Phylogenetic analysis shows that SpdA, SpdB, and SpdC are highly conserved across bacteria, with notable homologs including the well-characterized Bacillus subtilis sporulation factors PrkA (SpdA), YhbH (SpdB), and SpoVR (SpdC).
